prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That narrow cot, hardly any bigger than a child’s, is where Droste died (it’s there in her museum in Meersburg), on that sofa Hölderlin in his tower room at the carpenter’s, Rilke and George in hospital beds presumably, in Switzerland, in Weimar, Nietzsche’s great black eyes rested on white pillows till they looked their last— all of it junk now, or no longer extant, unattributable, anonymous in its insentient and continual disintegration. We bear within us the seeds of all the gods, the gene of death and the gene of love— who separated them, the words and things, who blended them, the torments and the place where they come to an end, the few boards and the floods of tears, home for a few wretched hours. Can be no sorrow. Too distant, too remote, bed and tears too impalpable, no No, no Yes, birth and bodily pain and faith an undefinable surge, a lurch, a power stirring in its sleep moved bed and tears— sleep well!

Hölderlin died on the sofa in his tower chamber at the carpenter’s house; Rilke and George, presumably, in hospital beds—in Switzerland, in Weimar—while Nietzsche’s immense dark eyes lay against white pillows until they closed forever. Today these objects are mere debris, if they survive at all: impossible to identify, without names, mindlessly and ceaselessly decaying. Inside us lie the beginnings of every god, the gene for dying beside the gene for loving. Who divided word from object, and who joined agony to the place where agony ceases—the handful of planks, the torrents of weeping, the shelter of a few miserable hours? Grief is impossible. Everything is too far away, too removed; bed and tears have lost all substance. Neither No nor Yes remains. Birth, physical suffering, and faith become an unnameable swell, a sudden staggering motion, some force half-awake that set bed and tears in motion—sleep peacefully.
outputs.L3:
The passage evokes the deathbeds of writers such as Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, Friedrich Hölderlin, Rainer Maria Rilke, Stefan George, and Friedrich Nietzsche. Once intimate objects associated with the final moments of these figures, the beds have since lost their immediate human significance. They have become museum exhibits, discarded furniture, or anonymous material subject to continual deterioration.

Against this image of physical decay, the text reflects on the complexity of human existence. Within every person lies an intertwined potential for divinity, death, and love—forces that cannot be neatly separated from one another. This entanglement prompts questions about how words become detached from things, how suffering relates to its ending, and how physical places become either divided from or fused with emotional pain.

Distance—whether temporal, spatial, or emotional—further transforms these experiences. Sorrow, birth, pain, and faith gradually become impalpable, losing the clarity and immediacy they once possessed. What remains is not a distinct memory or meaning, but an indefinable force moving beneath them: a persistent, elusive energy that survives even as objects decay and experiences recede.
outputs.L4:
### Mortality and Distance

The deaths of poets and philosophers often reach us as carefully preserved scenes: a dim room, a narrow bed, a final gesture, a sentence remembered by those who stood nearby. We imagine the failing bodies of those whose minds once seemed immense, and the contrast unsettles us. Their words may have crossed centuries, but their flesh remained subject to exhaustion, fever, silence, and decay. No brilliance could rescue them from the ordinary humiliations of dying. The poet who gave language to beauty and the philosopher who sought enduring truth both arrived at the same physical limit, where thought weakened, breath faltered, and the body ceased to obey the will.

Yet mortality is not merely an end imposed upon human life. It is woven into everything that makes life human. The body that can die is also the body that can desire, embrace, suffer, and believe. Our vulnerability gives intensity to love because every attachment may be broken; it gives urgency to faith because certainty remains beyond our reach. Pain reminds us that consciousness is rooted in flesh, while love persuades us that the self can extend beyond its own boundaries. Death, love, pain, and faith are therefore not separate powers but interdependent expressions of the same fragile existence.

To remember a death closely is to feel its particularity. A room retains the shape of the absent person. A chair, a window, or a fold in the bedclothes seems charged with meaning. Grief attaches itself to such details, insisting that this death was unlike any other because this person was unlike any other. Those who mourn may feel that the whole world has been altered, though beyond the walls life continues with indifference. Streets remain crowded, seasons turn, and distant people wake without knowing that anything has happened.

With time and distance, however, the sharpness of sorrow begins to fade. The deathbed becomes an anecdote, the room becomes a historical location, and the final words become a quotation whose certainty can no longer be verified. What was immediate passes into memory, then into legend. Even grief, which once appeared permanent, loses its precise edges. Distance does not prove that sorrow was false; it reveals how deeply sorrow depends upon presence—upon a voice, a face, and a body occupying a particular place.

Certainty dissolves in the same way. We cannot finally know what the dying perceived, whether they felt terror or peace, whether faith sustained them, or whether pain erased every thought. Testimony can preserve gestures and phrases, but it cannot enter the solitude of another person’s final consciousness. Death remains resistant to explanation. Philosophy may define it, religion may surround it with promise, and poetry may give it images, yet something essential remains unnamed.

Seen from afar, death loses its personal features and becomes a force moving briefly through the world. It enters a body, disturbs a household, darkens a room, and passes on. For a time, everything trembles around its presence: memory intensifies, love becomes desperate, and ordinary objects seem transformed. Then the disturbance subsides. The body grows still, the mourners depart, and the place returns to silence.

What remains is not an answer but an impression of immense impersonality. Death belongs to everyone and therefore to no one alone. It moves through famous lives and forgotten ones without distinction, touching genius and obscurity with the same indifferent hand. Afterward, the world closes over the event. The room darkens, the body rests, and sorrow itself eventually grows quiet, as though mortality were only a momentary stirring before all things settle once more into sleep.
outputs.L5:
### Droste und Meersburg

Meersburg am Bodensee ist eng mit der Dichterin Annette von Droste-Hülshoff verbunden. Ab 1841 hielt sie sich regelmäßig in der mittelalterlichen Stadt auf, wo ihre Schwester Jenny mit ihrem Mann Joseph von Laßberg auf der Alten Burg lebte. Die besondere Atmosphäre Meersburgs, der Blick über den See und die Nähe zu den Alpen inspirierten Droste zu zahlreichen literarischen Arbeiten.

1843 erwarb die Schriftstellerin das Fürstenhäusle, ein kleines Anwesen oberhalb der Stadt. Dort fand sie Ruhe zum Schreiben und einen Rückzugsort abseits des gesellschaftlichen Lebens. Heute erinnert das Droste-Museum im Fürstenhäusle an ihr Leben und Werk. Persönliche Gegenstände, Möbel und Manuskripte geben Einblick in die Welt einer der bedeutendsten deutschsprachigen Dichterinnen des 19. Jahrhunderts.

„That special feeling“ – jenes besondere Gefühl von Landschaft, Geschichte und Poesie – ist in Meersburg bis heute spürbar. Wer durch die engen Gassen geht, die Burg besucht oder vom Fürstenhäusle auf den Bodensee blickt, kann nachvollziehen, warum dieser Ort für Droste so wichtig war. Meersburg ist deshalb nicht nur ein beliebtes Reiseziel, sondern auch ein bedeutender Ort deutscher Literaturgeschichte.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose meditation on the deathbeds of famous German-language poets—Droste, Hölderlin, Rilke, George, and Nietzsche—exploring mortality, grief, and the decay of material objects.
counterfactuals.output:
Annette von Droste-Hülshoff died above Lake Constance, in Meersburg, where the water keeps its vast blue counsel beneath the windows. One imagines the room listening: the bedstead taking the slight weight of her body, the washbasin filmed with cold, a glass left half full, daylight fading on the wooden floor. Beyond the walls, the lake continued its ancient labor of appearing eternal. Yet even water decays into weather, even castles loosen grain by grain into dust. The hand that had summoned heaths, bells, marsh-lights, and hidden guilt could no longer lift itself. Objects remained faithful only in the way objects are faithful: by surviving without remembering.

Hölderlin’s bed stood in the tower at Tübingen, above the Neckar. For decades he had inhabited the long aftermath of himself, while seasons crossed the river and strangers climbed the stairs to look upon the poet as upon a ruin. The chair, the narrow table, the window opening toward poplars and water—these acquired the mute authority of relics even before he died. But a relic is merely decay granted a name. Wood splits; cloth pales; ink rusts into brown. The gods whom Hölderlin called near had always been departing. At the end, perhaps death was only the last of those divine distances, the final shore toward which the river had been carrying every reflected cloud.

Rilke died at Valmont, among the disciplined whiteness of the sanatorium, with the mountains keeping their terrible composure. His blood had become an invisible wound. The body, which in his poems was so often a vessel for angels, roses, panthers, torsos, and the pressure of the unsayable, had narrowed to pain beneath linen. A rose is said to have wounded him; whether legend or fact, the image persists because grief prefers a thorn it can touch. Yet the flower itself would have browned at the edges, collapsed inward, stained the water in its vase. Beauty does not defeat corruption. It makes corruption intimate. Petal, sheet, skin: each yields to the same dark chemistry.

Stefan George died in Minusio, far from the Germany that was already clothing catastrophe in banners and metal. Around the master, disciples had built an architecture of reverence, as though ceremony might seal a life against common extinction. But death enters every circle without initiation. It does not recognize rank, style, or the severe music of a name. The books on the table gather dust along their upper edges; the laurel dries and becomes brittle; the portrait silvering in its frame clouds slowly from within. Even marble, that favorite dream of permanence, is only stone consenting to weather.

Nietzsche’s last bed was in Weimar. By then the voice that had spoken in lightning had long been silent, and his body had become the helpless province of others. The philosopher of overcoming lay beyond argument, beyond pride, beyond the splendid cruelty of aphorism. Near him, perhaps, stood the ordinary furniture of illness: bottles, cloths, spoons, a basin, a clock. How unbearable that clocks continue beside the dying. Their hands advance with perfect indifference, dividing anguish into equal portions. Later the room becomes historical; the bed is preserved, the papers catalogued, the spectacles placed carefully beneath glass. But glass clouds. Leather flakes. Metal tarnishes. Archives, too, are mortal forests.

At every famous deathbed, grief performs the same mistaken inventory. Here is the pillow that held the head. Here is the pen. Here the cup touched by the mouth. We point because the person can no longer be pointed to. Matter becomes a poor grammar for absence. We ask the comb, the coat, the bedside table to decline the vanished name, but they know only the language of wear: fraying, fading, loosening, stain.

And still we keep them.

Not because they conquer death, but because they share it. The poet’s page yellows as the poet’s hand once yellowed; the house settles; the tower sheds plaster; the rose darkens in its vase. Material things console us by failing slowly. They make visible what the body knew at once: that form is a temporary gathering, that every object is already on its way from presence to trace.

The poems alone seem to escape, yet they escape imperfectly. Their words pass from mouth to mouth, altered by breath, by era, by grief. They survive not like monuments but like rivers—never the same substance, never entirely lost. Droste’s moor wind, Hölderlin’s departing gods, Rilke’s rose, George’s austere star, Nietzsche’s mountain air: they enter strangers and are changed.

Perhaps this is all immortality means. Not the preservation of the bed, the room, the bone, or the book, but the continual awakening of an old cadence in a mortal body. We read, and for a moment the dead borrow our lungs. Then we close the volume. Dust descends. Evening gathers at the window. The objects wait in their patient ruin, and somewhere, beyond possession, the words go on grieving us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental paragraph in the style of postwar German modernist literature, moving associatively from museum furniture and hospital beds to birth, love, death, faith, and sleep.
counterfactuals.output: The chair behind glass had forgotten the body, yet retained, in the shallow bruise of its cushion, a human absence; beside it the iron bedstead, white as a reprimand, repeated itself in the hospital corridor, where wheels whispered of departures and every sheet concealed either a birth or its reversal. We enter the world, the nurse said, as though entering a museum after closing, startled by the labels, the cold lamps, the unbearable antiquity of our own hands. Later we call this astonishment love and lie together to warm the exhibits; later still, death inventorying the room, we discover that nothing belonged to us—not the chair, not the child, not even the name God pinned crookedly beneath the heart. Faith is perhaps only the refusal to read that label. Sleep, meanwhile, lowers its blinds, smooths the hospital linen, seats the dead among the furniture, and rocks us, without explanation, toward morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a narrator visiting literary memorial sites in Germany and reflecting on the beds where canonical writers died. Make the language fragmented, philosophical, and emotionally detached.
counterfactuals.output:
In Weimar, the bed is smaller than expected.

White linen. A wooden frame. The pillow arranged beneath the idea of a head.

Goethe died here, they say. As if death remained loyal to furniture. As if the final breath had not dispersed long ago into plaster, curtains, the lungs of visitors.

Outside, buses turn in the square.

Later, in Marbach, another room. Schiller’s bed, narrow and elevated, resembles an instrument whose use has been forgotten. A rope barrier divides the living from the dead, though no one seems certain on which side the dead are standing.

The guide speaks of fever. Of manuscripts. Of the body’s betrayal.

I look at the blanket.

Wool persists longer than intention.

At Röcken, Nietzsche has no bed, only stone, grass, the proximity of a church. Yet I imagine one: the sheets damp, the philosopher already absent from the face bearing his name. Thought departing first. Flesh continuing out of habit.

Every memorial contains such errors.

A chair presented as witness.  
A window accused of having seen.  
A bed made innocent by restoration.

In Lübeck, rain gathers on the glass. Somewhere Thomas Mann’s characters are still dying with greater precision than Thomas Mann died. Literature corrects the body. The body offers no revision.

By evening, the rooms begin to merge.

Same pale wall. Same careful silence. Same rectangular vacancy where suffering has been curated into order.

One travels to find the dead and finds housekeeping.

The beds are always made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue about how the physical relics of dead authors become anonymous junk, while their beds evoke tears, bodily pain, and the inseparability of love and death.
counterfactuals.output:
They leave behind so many things.

A comb with three teeth missing.  
A tarnished spoon. Spectacles clouded with the weather  
of a vanished face. Receipts folded into quarters,  
a button in a drawer, the husk of a pen  
that once persuaded death to wait outside.

At first we label everything.

**His cup. Her shawl. The knife he used for pears.**  
We whisper provenance over each object  
like a charm against oblivion. But years loosen the names.  
The cup enters a box. The box enters a cellar.  
The cellar changes hands. Soon the spoon is only a spoon,  
the button only a small black moon  
no one remembers sewing.

This is how relics become rubbish:  
not through contempt, but through the patient labor of dust.

Yet the bed—

The bed refuses anonymity.

Stand beside it and the body understands  
before the mind can defend itself.  
Here was the weight of the shoulder.  
Here the knees drew up in fever.  
Here the spine, that ladder of suffering,  
lowered itself night after night.  
The mattress keeps its shallow geography:  
the valley of the hip, the hollow where a head  
argued with darkness, dreamed, woke, failed to wake.

And suddenly my own flesh aches.

My ribs tighten as if grief had fingers.  
My back recalls every hour spent beside the ill,  
every basin carried, every sheet changed quietly,  
every hand held past the point when touch could help.  
What is sorrow, if not the body’s knowledge  
that another body has been taken from it?

Perhaps that is why beds make us weep.  
They are altars built for two gods  
who have never been separable: love and death.

We lie down because we trust.  
We lie down because we are tired.  
We lie down beside someone and say, without speaking,  
Here is the place where I am most defenseless.  
Here is my breath. Here is my warmth.  
Here is the little death of sleep—  
promise me you will be here when I return.

But no one can promise.

The dead author’s manuscripts may fade,  
his ink become a brown rumor,  
her letters be sold, misfiled, quoted badly.  
The chair will forget the shape of genius.  
The coat will lose its shoulders.  
Every cherished object will drift at last  
toward the vast republic of nameless things.

But the bed remembers what fame cannot:  
that the hand which wrote was sometimes cold,  
that the mouth which made immortal sentences  
once cried out in pain, once kissed, once begged  
for one more hour.

I stand there, and I do not mourn the books.

I mourn the warm animal who made them—  
the one who loved under these blankets,  
who suffered against this pillow,  
who entered sleep each night rehearsing death,  
and who, because love had lain beside them,  
could never meet death alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense stream-of-consciousness passage beginning with Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s cot in Meersburg, then invoking Hölderlin, Rilke, Stefan George, and Nietzsche before ending with the words “sleep well!”
counterfactuals.output: Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s cot in Meersburg, narrow as a pause between two clauses, still seems to hold the shape of an exhausted sentence, lake-light trembling over its linen while the old castle walls inhale dust, ink, fever, and the muffled footfall of poems that refused the grave; and from the tower Hölderlin turns toward the impossible river, addressing gods who have already withdrawn behind the blue machinery of noon, while Rilke, listening at every locked door, hears an angel’s terrible wing brush the roses, the mirrors, the small animal heart curled in its own darkness; then Stefan George enters with ceremonial steps, bearing the cold lamp of a secret kingdom, each syllable robed, each silence disciplined, though beneath the marble vowels something mortal knocks and knocks; and Nietzsche, suddenly laughing on the mountain, shatters the lamp, blesses the fragments, commands the abyss to dance, until lake, tower, rose, mask, and cot revolve together in the sleepless skull, where Annette opens her eyes once more, not waking, not dead, only listening as language draws the blanket to her chin and whispers: sleep well!
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
